corpus_definition: To show or tell someone how to perform a task.

forms.definition: information that tells you how to do or use something
forms.example: Read the instructions carefully before you use the new washing machine.
forms.note: Usually plural when it means steps to follow: 'follow the instructions'.

syn.note: Plural noun with the same meaning: 'Follow the directions on the box.'
Help and advice about what to do; more general and uncountable.
The work of a teacher in general, not one set of steps.

forms.definition: to show or tell someone how to do a task
forms.example: The coach will instruct the team on tactics before the match.
forms.note: It can also mean 'to order': 'She instructed him to wait outside.'

syn.note: Everyday word; instruct is more formal and often about a practical skill.
Teach a skill through practice over a period of time.
Easy word: 'Can you show me how to do it?'
Tell people what to do; more about giving orders than teaching.

forms.definition: giving useful information that helps you learn something
forms.example: The museum visit was very instructive for the children.

syn.note: Giving a lot of useful facts; very close in meaning.
Helping people learn; common for films, games and trips.
Easy, general word: helpful in any way, not only for learning.

forms.definition: made to teach people how to do something
forms.example: We watched an instructional video about first aid.

forms.note: There is no common adverb in this family; 'instructively' exists but is very rare.

people.definition: a person whose job is to teach a practical skill such as driving
people.example: My driving instructor is very patient and calm.

context.text: My driving instructor instructed me to check the mirrors before every turn. His instructions were short and clear, so I passed my test in Tashkent the first time.

reviewer_note: Mapped the teaching sense; the 'order someone' sense is mentioned only in a note on the verb.

corpus_definition: Paying to protect yourself against loss or damage.

forms.definition: an agreement where you pay a company and it pays you after loss or damage
forms.example: Do you have car insurance for this vehicle?

syn.note: British English, used in business: 'travel cover'.
Mostly American English: 'health coverage'.
General word for keeping something safe; not always a paid agreement.
The written contract you get from the company: 'an insurance policy'.

forms.definition: to pay a company so it will pay you if something is lost or damaged
forms.example: We insured our new car against theft and accidents.
forms.note: Do not mix it up with 'ensure' (make sure). In American English 'insure' is sometimes used for 'ensure' too.

syn.note: Used with the company as subject: 'The policy covers fire and flood.'
Keep something safe in any way, not only by paying a company.

forms.definition: protected by an agreement that pays you after loss or damage
forms.example: Is your house insured against fire?

syn.note: Everyday way to say the same thing: 'Are you covered?'
Kept safe in a general way, not only by a paid agreement.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a company or person that sells protection against loss or damage
people.example: The insurer paid for the repairs after the accident.

context.text: My father insured his car last month. The insurance costs about 800,000 som a year, but if there is an accident, the insurer pays for the repairs.

reviewer_note: insure vs ensure trap explained in the verb note; uninsured kept as an antonym, not a form.

corpus_definition: To mix different groups of people or things together.

forms.definition: the process of bringing different people or things together as one group
forms.example: The integration of new students into the school took only a few weeks.

syn.note: Making sure everyone is part of a group; often used about people.
Things put together; does not say they work well as one.
Easy word for putting things or people together.

ant.note: Keeping groups of people apart, often by law or rules.

forms.definition: to join different people or things together so they work as one
forms.example: New students quickly integrated into the school group.

syn.note: Put two or more things together; used more for things than people.
Easy, everyday word for putting things or people together.
Join together for a shared goal; stronger and more formal.
Easy word: become part of a group: 'He joined our team.'

ant.note: Keep or move people or things apart.
Keep groups apart on purpose; a strong, formal word.

forms.definition: with different parts or people joined well together as one
forms.example: The city has an integrated bus and metro system with one ticket.

syn.note: Made into one whole; a little formal.
Put together, but the parts may still be separate.
With different kinds of people or things: 'a mixed class'.

ant.note: Not joined to the other parts.

forms.note: Integral (= a necessary part of a whole) shares an old Latin root but is not made from integrate.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Three students from Samarkand joined our class this year. They integrated quickly because our teacher believes integration starts with team games. Now we feel like one integrated group.

reviewer_note: Only the joining-groups sense mapped; integral and integrity share an old root but are not made from integrate, so they are left out.

corpus_definition: the mental ability to learn and understand new things.

forms.definition: the ability to learn, understand and think about things well
forms.example: The professor is known for her high intelligence.
forms.note: It also means secret information about an enemy ('military intelligence'); that meaning is not shown here.

syn.note: Everyday word; intelligence sounds more serious and scientific.
Informal: 'She has brains.'
Good judgement from experience; a clever young person may not have it yet.

ant.note: Lack of the ability to think well; a strong, rude word about people.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: able to learn and understand things quickly and well
forms.example: Dolphins are very intelligent animals.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning (more British).
Easy, everyday word; very common in American English.
Often used about children and students: 'a bright pupil'.

ant.note: Not able to think well; can be rude about people.
More formal and polite than stupid.

forms.definition: in a clever way that shows good thinking
forms.example: She answered the difficult question intelligently.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little less formal.
With good judgement, often from experience.
In a practical, reasonable way.

ant.note: In a way that shows bad thinking.

context.text: Dilnoza's intelligence surprised her teachers in Namangan. She always answers questions intelligently, and everyone agrees she is a very intelligent girl.

reviewer_note: Secret-information sense (military intelligence) noted on the noun but not mapped; no -ence affix claimed (intelligent/intelligence split is not clean).

corpus_definition: A short period of time between two events.

forms.definition: a period of time between two events or two parts of a show
forms.example: There was a long interval between the two acts of the play.
forms.note: In a theatre, British English says 'interval' and American English says 'intermission'. 'At intervals' means 'regularly, with time between'.

syn.note: Easy word for a short rest between two activities.
A short stop, usually shorter than an interval.
Space or time between two things: 'a gap of two years'.
American English for the break in a play or concert.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family; use the phrase 'at intervals'.

context.text: The concert had a twenty-minute interval, so we went out for tea. On the way home, buses to Chilonzor came at intervals of ten minutes.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; British/American difference (interval vs intermission) noted.

corpus_definition: When an army enters a country to take control by force.

forms.definition: the act of an army entering another country to take control by force
forms.example: The country prepared for the invasion at the border.
forms.note: Also used for things that come in large numbers or are not wanted: 'an invasion of tourists', 'an invasion of privacy'.

syn.note: More general: an attack can be short and does not always mean taking control.
Staying in and controlling a country after entering it.
A short, quick attack; the attackers leave again.

ant.note: When an army leaves a country or area.
When an army moves back because it is losing.

forms.definition: to enter a country with an army to take control of it
forms.example: Genghis Khan's army invaded Central Asia in the 13th century.

syn.note: More general; you can attack without entering or taking control.
Get control of a place or company; not always by force.
Stay in a place and control it, usually after invading.

ant.note: Take an army out of a country.
Move back away from the enemy.

forms.definition: spreading quickly into places where it is not wanted and causing harm
forms.example: This invasive plant is killing the trees along the river.
forms.note: Belongs to invade = spread into a place (plants, illness) or go into the body in medicine, not armies. For armies, say 'the invading army'.
There is no common adverb in this family.

people.definition: a soldier, army or country that enters another country by force
people.example: The people of the city fought bravely against the invaders.

context.text: In history class we read about the Mongol invasion of Central Asia. The invaders came from the east and invaded Samarkand and Bukhara in 1220.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR B2); invasive is other_meaning (plants/medicine), not the army sense.

corpus_definition: A thing that someone created for the very first time.

forms.definition: a new thing or machine that someone makes for the first time
forms.example: The light bulb was a great invention.
forms.note: It can also mean the act of making something new: 'the invention of the telephone'.

syn.note: Something made by someone; can be art or food, not only a machine.
A new idea or way of doing things; common in business and technology.
A machine or tool for a special job; it may not be new.
Careful: you discover something that already exists, but you make an invention.

forms.definition: to make or design something that did not exist before
forms.example: Who invented the first computer?
forms.note: It can also mean to make up a story or excuse that is not true.

syn.note: Make something new; more general than invent.
Easy phrasal verb, used more for ideas and plans.
Plan how something will look and work, before it is made.

forms.definition: good at thinking of new and clever ideas
forms.example: She is an inventive cook who mixes Uzbek and Korean dishes.

syn.note: Very close; the most common everyday word.
Good at having new, unusual ideas.
New and different from anything before.

ant.note: Not able to think of new or interesting ideas.

forms.definition: in a new and clever way
forms.example: The old factory was inventively turned into a modern art gallery.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common.
In a way that shows new, unusual ideas.

people.definition: a person who makes or designs something completely new
people.example: Thomas Edison was a famous American inventor.

context.text: Ali's grandfather was an inventor in Fergana. His best invention was a small machine for cleaning cotton. He was always inventive and never stopped trying new ideas.

reviewer_note: discovery is kept only as a 'related' word with a warning note (discover existing things vs invent new ones).

corpus_definition: to use money to earn more money in the future

forms.definition: money that you put into something to get more money later
forms.example: Buying land near the city was a good investment.

syn.note: Money given for a project; the giver may not want profit.
The part of a business that you own because you put money into it.

forms.definition: to put money into a business or plan to make more money later
forms.example: She decided to invest her savings in new stocks.
forms.note: Pattern: invest (money) in something. It can also mean to give time or effort: 'invest time in your studies'.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Give money for a project; you may not expect profit back.
Careful: when you spend money it is gone; when you invest, you hope to get more back.

ant.note: Take your money out of a bank or business.

forms.definition: caring a lot about something because you have given it time or feelings
forms.example: She is very invested in her students' success.
forms.note: Belongs to invest = give time, effort or feelings, not money. Informal and fairly new.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person or company that puts money into something to make a profit
people.example: Foreign investors are building a new hotel in Khiva.

context.text: My uncle invested his savings in a small bakery in Bukhara. It was a good investment, and now other investors want to join him.

reviewer_note: Money sense mapped; the time/feelings sense appears only as the other_meaning adjective 'invested'.

corpus_definition: To look for facts about a crime or a problem.

forms.definition: an official search for the facts about a crime or problem
forms.example: The investigation into the fire took three weeks.

syn.note: An official search for facts; British English also spells it 'enquiry'.
Used mostly in newspapers and news reports.
A careful look at something; not always about a crime.
Careful study to learn new facts, usually in science or at university.

forms.definition: to try to find out the facts about a crime or problem
forms.example: The police will investigate the cause of the fire.

syn.note: Easy phrasal verb with the same meaning.
Look at something very carefully.
Learn about something new; less about crimes.
Easy word: look quickly to see if something is right.

ant.note: Pay no attention to a problem at all.

forms.definition: trying to find hidden facts, especially in news reporting
forms.example: She works as an investigative journalist for a news website.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person whose job is to find out the facts about crimes or problems
people.example: A private investigator followed the man for two days.

context.text: The police are investigating a robbery at the Chorsu market. A young investigator found a camera video, but the investigation may take two more weeks.

reviewer_note: Not part of the invest family: investigate comes from a different Latin root (vestigium), so no cross-links to invest/investment.

corpus_definition: Giving money to something to get more money later.

forms.definition: money that you put into something to get more money later
forms.example: This house is a good long-term investment.
forms.note: Also used for time or effort that will help you later: 'Learning English is a good investment.'

syn.note: Money given for a project; the giver may not want profit.
The part of a business that you own because you put money into it.

forms.definition: to put money into a business or plan to make more money later
forms.example: Many families invest in flats and land.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Give money for a project; you may not expect profit back.
Careful: when you spend money it is gone; when you invest, you hope to get more back.

ant.note: Take your money out of a bank or business.

forms.definition: caring a lot about something because you have given it time or feelings
forms.example: The players are really invested in winning this cup.
forms.note: Belongs to invest = give time, effort or feelings, not money. Informal and fairly new.
There is no adverb in this family.

people.definition: a person or company that puts money into something to make a profit
people.example: The investors met in Tashkent to discuss the new factory.

context.text: Buying a flat in Tashkent is a popular investment. Many families invest in property, and some investors buy two or three flats.

reviewer_note: Headword is the noun; invest is the derivational verb it is made from. Time/feelings sense shown only as other_meaning 'invested'.
